title: Koepp et al. 1998, Nature 393:266-8 (abstract via PubMed efetch)
label: research
claim: 11C-raclopride PET: striatal raclopride binding fell during a video game vs baseline (read as dopamine release), correlated positively with performance, greatest in ventral striatum. Abstract gives no n or effect size.

title: Koepp et al. 1998 full text (copy of the paper, pdftotext)
label: research
claim: Eight healthy right-handed male volunteers; tank-steering game for monetary incentive in first 50 min of scan. Binding potential reduced, ANOVA F=7.72, P<0.01; ventral striatum mean -13% (range +8 to -42%); authors cite 1% binding drop = at least 8% rise in extracellular dopamine (calibrated from amphetamine work). Compared with amphetamine -16%, methylphenidate -23%. Baseline was a blank-screen scan and payment was 7 pounds per game level reached, so game, money and motor task are confounded; one task, n=8, men only.

title: Egerton et al. 2009, The dopaminergic basis of human behaviors: a review of molecular imaging studies, Neurosci Biobehav Rev (PMC copy)
label: research
claim: Review incl. the Koepp group's own reanalysis (first 100k of 315k chars read): without head-movement correction and with a fixed 40% threshold ROI, published result may be biased; with anatomical ROIs right ventral striatum about -7.3% stayed significant, left only trend; with frame-by-frame motion correction regional changes were much smaller and nonsignificant; correlation with performance disappeared after ROI redefinition. Authors conclude head movement may have biased the published results. No direct replication of the game task identified in the portion read. A later verification read of the same PMC text (2026-11-08) found the overall effect of condition stayed significant after motion correction, while per-region changes did not.

title: Schultz, Dayan & Montague 1997, A neural substrate of prediction and reward, Science (abstract via PubMed efetch)
label: research
claim: Primate dopaminergic neurons' fluctuating output 'apparently signals changes or errors in the predictions of future salient and rewarding events'; framed with learning theory. Monkey single-neuron recording, not human, not games.

title: Fiorillo, Tobler & Schultz 2003, Discrete coding of reward probability and uncertainty by dopamine neurons, Science (abstract)
label: research
claim: Phasic dopamine response varied monotonically with reward probability (prediction-error coding); a separate sustained ramp covaried with uncertainty, maximal at P=0.5. Monkey data; relevant to why uncertainty may matter, but does not measure enjoyment.

title: Berridge & Robinson 1998, What is the role of dopamine in reward: hedonic impact, reward learning, or incentive salience? (abstract)
label: research
claim: Review plus rat study (dopamine depleted up to 99% in accumbens/neostriatum by 6-OHDA; taste-reactivity unchanged): concludes dopamine is not needed for hedonic pleasure or hedonic learning; may mediate incentive salience, 'wanting' not 'liking'. Rat data; the authors frame it as a hypothesis.

title: Scientific American, Dopamine: The Currency of Desire (science journalism quoting researchers)
label: verbatim
claim: Volkow (NIDA): 'Dopamine is not the pleasure molecule in the simple, direct way it is typically portrayed in the media.' Schultz: dopamine 'encodes the difference between what you're getting and what you have expected.' Berridge/Robinson: wanting vs liking. Article concludes 'many experts think that each captures some element of the truth' (prediction error vs wanting may operate on different timescales). Journalism, not a primary source; quotes are the value.

title: Kuhn et al. 2011, The neural basis of video gaming, Transl Psychiatry (abstract)
label: research
claim: Cross-sectional MRI, 154 14-year-olds: frequent gamers had higher left (ventral) striatal grey matter volume, correlated with shorter deliberation time in a gambling task; enhanced striatal activity at feedback of loss in MID task. Authors say it 'could reflect altered reward processing and represent adaptive neural plasticity'. Correlational; cannot say gaming caused it; says nothing about dopamine release or about fun.

title: Kuhn et al. 2014, Playing Super Mario induces structural brain plasticity, Mol Psychiatry (abstract)
label: research
claim: Training study, 2 months, at least 30 min/day vs control: grey-matter increase in right hippocampus, right DLPFC, bilateral cerebellum (not striatum). HC and DLPFC gains correlated with desire for gaming. Not a dopamine measure.

title: Lazzaro 2004/5, Why We Play Games: Four Keys to More Emotion Without Story (XEODesign white paper v2.01, pdftotext of PDF)
label: practitioner
claim: Field study of 30 adult players (15 hardcore, 15 casual), 90-120 min each, plus interviews with 15 non-players; Contextual Inquiry + proprietary XEOAnalysis; 45 h video, over 2,000 observations sorted into affinity groups. Paper states 'It is beyond the methodology and scope of this study to produce statistically significant results'. Four Keys (Hard, Easy, Serious, People Fun) chosen by 4 criteria incl. 'already present in ultra popular games'; claim that best sellers hit at least three of four keys rests on a handful of named titles. Commercial firm, qualitative, selected rather than derived, not peer-reviewed.

title: Hunicke, LeBlanc & Zubek, MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research (pdftotext)
label: practitioner
claim: Lists eight aesthetics (Sensation, Fantasy, Narrative, Challenge, Fellowship, Discovery, Expression, Submission) as vocabulary replacing 'fun'; says 'there is no Grand Unified Theory of games or formula' for fun; used to describe games and why they appeal to different players. A descriptive taxonomy with no empirical test in the paper.

title: Malone & Levin 1983 conference report (secondary account of Malone 1980/1981)
label: research
claim: Report says Malone ran a survey of children's computer-game preferences and two experiments that removed features one at a time from games (Breakout; Darts for fractions) to see which mattered, then proposed challenge (uncertain-outcome goals; variable difficulty, multiple-level goals), fantasy (intrinsic beats extrinsic, hypothesised), curiosity. Survey/experiment numbers not in this source and not found elsewhere; second-hand.

title: Malone 1981, Toward a theory of intrinsically motivating instruction (Cognitive Science 4:333-369), full PDF read
label: research
claim: Three studies, all with children or students on 1970s computer games. (1) Survey: 65 elementary pupils (42 boys, 23 girls, K-8, about 25% of one private school) rated 25 games 0-3; no game got more than 17% of first places; test-retest on 4 children: 71% identical. Games were then coded for features and correlated with average rating (Table 3): goal r=.65 (p<.01), computer keeps a score .56, audio effects .51, randomness .48 (all p<.01), speed of answers counts .36, graphic game .38, word game -.38 (p<.05), visual effects .34, competition .31, variable difficulty .17, math game -.20, cooperation .02, fantasy .06 (all n.s.). Malone's own caveat: correlational, depends on the sample of games, cannot show cause. So in the survey fantasy and variable difficulty did not predict popularity; goal, score, audio and randomness did. (2) Breakout, 10 Stanford undergraduates (8 men, 2 women; 3 more discarded for not learning the game), six versions varying bricks breaking, ball bouncing off paddle, score; ratings 1-5: original 4.8, no score 4.1, no bricks 3.3, no bounce with score 2.1, no bricks no score 2.0, no bounce no score 1.4; version effect F(5,p)=25.84 p<.001; regression betas: breaking bricks .77, score .32, bounce .30, multiple R .87. Malone's reading: a clear goal mattered; versions with neither score nor bricks were significantly worse. (3) Darts (fractions): 80 fifth graders, 10 per condition, 8 versions each adding one feature (drill; +performance feedback; +score; +constructive feedback; +extrinsic fantasy; +music; +graphic representation; +intrinsic fantasy), free choice between Darts and Hangman over two 20-minute sessions. Condition effect on time F(7,48)=4.90 p<.001 and on liking F(7,48)=2.21 p<.05, plus a condition x sex interaction on time F(7,48)=4.84 p<.001; cells of 4-6 after pooling schools. Combined boys and girls: only significant step was liking rising when extrinsic fantasy was added (p<.05). By sex: girls spent less time on the original intrinsic-fantasy version (19.8 min) than on the extrinsic-fantasy-with-graphics version (29.8 min, p<.01); boys liked extrinsic fantasy (5.0 vs 3.6 liking, p<.05); boys' dislike of verbal constructive feedback and girls' liking of music were not significant in the regression or utility analysis, which Malone calls less reliable; adding performance feedback to the drill made no significant difference. The challenge, fantasy and curiosity theory is a hypothesis built after these studies: curiosity was not tested, and the data do not show intrinsic fantasy beating extrinsic (the opposite for girls). Small samples, one game each, 1970s text and graphics, and the survey, Breakout and Darts samples differ.

title: Mekler, Bopp, Tuch & Opwis 2014, A systematic review of quantitative studies on the enjoyment of digital entertainment games, CHI 2014 pp.927-936 (record page, summarised)
label: research
claim: Reviewed 87 quantitative studies (search window 2008-2012 per a later review). Frames enjoyment as the valence of player experience; 'enjoyment is distinct from flow in that it may occur independently of challenge and cognitive involvement'; links enjoyment to need/value satisfaction; flags methodological problems. Full text not read.

title: Law, Brühlmann & Mekler 2018, Systematic Review and Validation of the GEQ, CHI PLAY 2018 pp.257-270 (bibliographic record + search summary of OSF abstract)
label: snippet
claim: Per search summary of the OSF abstract (not seen directly): reviewed 73 GEQ publications, found inconsistent reporting and misleading citation of source and item counts; validation sample N=633 found no evidence for the originally postulated 7-factor structure; GEQ has no peer-reviewed origin paper. Needs primary check before quoting.

title: Deterding & Cutting 2023, Objective difficulty-skill balance impacts perceived balance but not behaviour, PACM HCI (CHI PLAY 2023)
label: research
claim: Preregistered, n=309, Go-like game vs AI set to win/draw/lose, five matches each: AI manipulated balance, draw rated most balanced, but balance did not affect play behaviour and the predicted inverted-U with positive play experience was not found. Authors say flow and SDT are too underspecified to test severely; suggest appraisals, novelty, progress matter. One game, one task, short sessions.

title: Koster, A Theory of Fun for Game Design: third-party summaries (Shortform, reading notes)
label: snippet
claim: Summaries say fun = the brain's reward for learning patterns, boredom when pattern is mastered or absent/over your head; Koster quoted 'learning is the drug' and a Shortform paraphrase makes it a dopamine claim. Book text not read; no data in a practitioner book to my knowledge (unverified).

title: Kao et al. CHI 2024, How does juicy game feedback motivate? (already a row in evidence/feedback.jsonl; abstract and search summary only here)
label: research
claim: Preregistered, 1,699 participants: curiosity the strongest predictor of enjoyment and the only predictor of free-choice playtime; uncertain success raised curiosity; amplified feedback reduced motives. Supports curiosity over mastery or effectance as the playtime driver in one action RPG.

title: Search-result summary of 'dopamine loop / variable ratio' commentary and loot-box literature
label: snippet
claim: Search surfaced: variable-ratio and rarity features are common in top mobile games (DiGRA descriptive paper, 85% each, not a player-outcome test); loot-box scoping review calls for longitudinal/experimental work; dopamine-specific claims in popular articles cite no primary player study. A Substack claim of a rat study showing amphetamine-like sensitisation is unverified.

title: Bartle 1996, Hearts, Clubs, Diamonds, Spades (Journal of MUD Research 1(1))
label: practitioner
claim: Four types on two axes, built from a 1989-90 debate among experienced players on one UK MUD; Bartle: 'I am not a trained psychologist, do not expect a conventionally rigorous approach.' Claims are about how type populations affect each other in a MUD (more killers drive out socialisers). Untested in the paper; silent on non-MUD games.

title: Bartle 2009, Understanding the Limits of Theory (in Bateman ed., Beyond Game Design)
label: verbatim
claim: Primary statement of limits (read via pdftotext, searched by keyword, not every page). Abstract: model 'is frequently misunderstood and misapplied'. 'It only applies to people who play virtual worlds for fun.' 'the model does not apply to people who play things other than virtual worlds for fun. More appropriate theories exist that should be used even for related game formats... or for games in general [Koster 05]'. It is a model you can 'run' to predict how a world turns out under different player-type balances, not a checkbox system: 'it's not simply a check-box system that says there are these categories of player and you need content for them all - if that's what you want, go with a taxonomy such as [Yee 07] instead.' 'The player types theory explains why people play virtual worlds, but not what they do.' On profiling: 'You will not be able to guarantee that any individual matching a particular profile will be of the type that the profile predicts.'

title: Yee 2006, The Demographics, Motivations, and Derived Experiences of Users of MMOGs (Presence 15(3))
label: research
claim: Self-selected online survey, ~30,000 MMORPG players over 3 years. EFA: 8 factors (44.5% variance), 5 usable motivation factors: Achievement, Relationship, Immersion, Escapism, Manipulation. Male (n=5,939) vs female (n=736) effect sizes r: Achievement .20, Relationship .15, Manipulation .15, Immersion .05, Escapism .05. Age vs weekly hours r=-.04 (mean 22 hrs/wk). Author limitation: self-selected, probably more engaged players; bias hits frequencies more than correlations. MMORPG only; factors are continuous scores, not exclusive types.

title: Yee DiGRA 2005 / CyberPsychology & Behavior 2006 'Motivations for play in online games' (search snippets)
label: snippet
claim: Secondary: 3 components (achievement: advancement, mechanics, competition; social: socializing, relationship, teamwork; immersion: discovery, role-playing, customization, escapism) from 10 subcomponents; DiGRA 2005 version PCA, eigenvalue>1 explaining 60% variance. N reported secondhand as ~3,000. Primary paper not read.

title: Yee, Ducheneaut, Nelson 2012, Online gaming motivations scale: development and validation (CHI 2012)
label: snippet
claim: Abstract via search: scale on a 3-factor model; 2,072 US participants and 645 Hong Kong/Taiwan participants for cross-cultural check; predictive validity against logged in-game behaviour. Secondary note says based on World of Warcraft players. Effect sizes not seen.

title: Quantic Foundry Gamer Motivation Model (search snippets; reference PDF and Medium post returned 403)
label: snippet
claim: 12 motivations in 6 pairs under 3 groups; sample claims vary by source (30,000+ 2015, 400,000+ 2019, 2M+ homepage). Secondhand reports: Completion most age-stable and higher in women; Challenge only motivation that resurges after 45; factor structure same across regions. Company data, not peer-reviewed in what I saw; effect sizes not obtained.

title: Hamari & Tuunanen 2014, Player Types: A Meta-synthesis (ToDiGRA 1(2))
label: research
claim: Literature search, then concept-centric synthesis of prior typologies: 'player types in previous literature can be synthesized into seven primary dimensions': Intensity, Achievement, Exploration, Sociability, Domination, Immersion, In-game demographics. Count of typologies not on the page.

title: Tondello et al. 2019 IJHCS, Empirical validation of the Gamification User Types Hexad scale in English and Spanish
label: research
claim: Three studies; 'Our findings support the structural validity of the scale', with improvements possible; some user types more common than others; gender and age associated with type profile. n per study not seen. A search summary (snippet) says an HCII 2021 study (n=1,073) found Hexad useful for identifying types with model fit needing work, and Hexad-12 (CHI 2023) improved fit.

title: Tondello & Nacke 2020, Frontiers in Computer Science: customizing gameful elements vs generic
label: research
claim: Two studies, 252 total (198 MTurk, 99/condition; 54 social media, 27/condition), image-tagging task. Customized (choose elements) vs generic (all 8 elements). Hexad links to element choice only partly supported: Badges/Challenges/Chance with Achiever, Leaderboards/Challenges with Player; many predicted relations unsupported; post-use preference ratings did not correlate with Hexad scores. Study 1: customized tagged more images (median 26 vs 14.5, p=.013) but fewer tags per image (4 vs 5, p=.008); no IMI difference. Study 2 image count n.s. (p=.064). Study 2 attrition high (54 of 127 finished). Discussion section not read.

title: Altmeyer et al. 2020 CHI PLAY, HexArcade (search snippet)
label: snippet
claim: N=147; participants mostly interacted with game elements matching their Hexad type, but behavioural predictive models did not explain enough variance to predict Hexad type reliably.

title: Busch et al. 2016 CHI EA, Player Type Models: Towards Empirical Validation
label: research
claim: Two online studies n1=592, n2=243 on BrainHex; psychometric properties (factor structure, reliability, stability) 'could be improved'; recommend revising the questionnaire. Abstract gives no loadings or reliabilities.

title: Busch et al., Using Player Type Models for Personalized Game Design: An Empirical Investigation
label: research
claim: Field study, 51 participants, mobile game built for BrainHex Mastermind and Seeker. 'Player type scores do not significantly predict player experience of according game mechanics.' Concludes models need improvement before supporting personalized games. Small n, one game.

title: Search listing mentioning Tondello, Nacke et al. IJHCI 2018 (BrainHex trait model)
label: snippet
claim: Search summary: BrainHex described by its authors as an interim model lacking validated psychometrics; survey of 50,000+ respondents yielded three trait dimensions: action, aesthetic, goal orientation. Primary paper not opened.

title: Hunicke, LeBlanc, Zubek 2004, MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research
label: developer
claim: Mechanics (data and algorithms), Dynamics (run-time behaviour of mechanics on player input), Aesthetics ('desirable emotional responses evoked in the player'). Designer sees M->D->A; player sees A->D->M. Eight aesthetics, stated as 'not limited to' this taxonomy: Sensation, Fantasy, Narrative, Challenge, Fellowship, Discovery, Expression, Submission. Says it is a tool for designers, researchers and scholars; says players' appeal varies by aesthetic. Contains no empirical test; developed in GDC Game Design and Tuning workshop 2001-04. The paper's own example games list 'Competition' beside the eight, i.e. list is open.

title: Walk, From MDA to DDE (Game Developer)
label: practitioner
claim: Critique by a producer/narrative designer: no place for narrative design; 'Every attempt to apply MDA to narrative design rules stretches MDA to the breaking point'; '90 % of MDA mechanics are not actually mechanical'; 'aesthetics' ambiguous. Credits dynamics as MDA's strength. Proposes DDE (Design: blueprint/mechanics/interface; Dynamics; Experience). Argument only, no data; DDE unfinished by his own account.

title: Wikipedia MDA framework (search snippet)
label: opinion
claim: Notes MDA criticised for neglecting many design aspects and focusing on mechanics; a Korean gamification study said MDA does not sufficiently reflect experience-oriented design. Not verified at source.

title: Kim, The compulsion loop explained (GameAnalytics)
label: practitioner
claim: Definition adapted from Adam Crowe: 'A habitual, designed chain of activities that will be repeated to gain a neurochemical reward.' 'The core loop is the chain of activities associated with the primary user flow'; compulsion loop is the deliberate design of that chain to condition behaviour; steps are anticipation, action, reward. Scientific basis cited is Skinner animal work and a Wikipedia dopamine entry; examples only (Clash of Clans, Farmville); retention claims carry no data.

title: Hopson 2001, Behavioral Game Design (Gamasutra; search snippet of page)
label: developer
claim: Bungie user researcher: schedules of reinforcement applied to game contingencies; variable ratio produces highest rates of activity, hence designers favour it. Page not fully read.

title: Hopson 2012 reply to Skinner-box critics (Game Developer)
label: developer
claim: Hopson: critics 'completely miss the point of the Skinner Box'; 'A Skinner Box is completely unnecessary to create operant conditioning'; contingencies are ethical 'if the designer believes the player will have more fun by fulfilling the contingency.' Short page; does not claim schedules alone make a game engaging.

title: Kao 2012, Reward Preference in Video Games (Princeton MSE thesis, adviser Yael Niv)
label: research
claim: Custom-built game; participants chose between game worlds. 'variable reward schedules were preferred to fixed reward schedules with the same mean, except when the variable schedule's range was extended.' Measures preference, not retention or play time. Master's thesis; n not extracted. Notes variable-ratio may not be preferred in games (cites unpredictability).

title: Tyack & Mekler 2020 CHI, SDT in HCI Games Research: Current Uses and Open Questions
label: research
claim: Reviewed 110 CHI and CHI PLAY papers citing SDT. Need satisfaction and intrinsic motivation most used; 'prominent core concepts and mini-theories are rarely considered explicitly, and few papers engage with SDT beyond descriptive accounts.' 82.73% treated SDT mainly descriptively; 61.82% studied player experience; PENS used in 40.00%, competence 38.18%, autonomy 36.36% dimensions. Review of usage, not a test of whether SDT predicts game outcomes.

title: Tyack & Mekler 2024, SDT and HCI Games Research: Unfulfilled Promises and Unquestioned Paradigms (TOCHI)
label: research
claim: First 100k of 422k characters read. 259 HCI games papers: 54.83% descriptive, 37.07% analytic, 8.11% generative; only 6 critiquing. 54.05% used an SDT instrument (IMI 31.66%, PENS 25.87%). PENS: proprietary items, at least three versions used, immersion subscale collapsed in all known studies, the claimed ~2,000-player CFA 'was never published'; PXI said to have more consistently solid psychometrics. GDC analysis (N=16 talks): practitioners know SDT concepts but HCI SDT literature is nearly absent from practitioner discourse. Recommends deliberate use and 'talking back' to theory.
